prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why neither small-vessel disease (Fazekas 2, lobar frontal and anterior temporal atrophy out of proportion) nor his remote alcohol use disorder (12 years sober, normal mammillary bodies and thalami) accounts for the progressive behavioural syndrome.
Treat the vascular comorbidity as a contributor: blood pressure control (142/88 mmHg in clinic), glycaemic control (HbA1c 7.8%) and continued CPAP.
Address safety and capacity: driving, access to firearms (retired police sergeant), finances (the $22,000 withdrawals), and lasting power of attorney while he can still take part.
Arrange caregiver education and support, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET, or perfusion SPECT where FDG-PET is unavailable, is the functional study when one is needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, sporadic, with concurrent small-vessel cerebrovascular disease (secondary contributor)

differential.key_features: For: hypertension, diabetes, Fazekas 2 white matter disease. Against: no infarct, a lobar frontal and anterior temporal atrophy pattern, and a behavioural syndrome that small-vessel disease does not produce; it is a contributor, not the cause.

differential.diagnosis: Alcohol-related brain damage or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
differential.key_features: For: remote alcohol use disorder, mildly wide-based gait. Against: 12 years sober, onset long after cessation, normal MCV, normal mammillary bodies and thalami, a disinhibited rather than amnestic profile.
For: mildly reduced memory. Against: frontal-predominant atrophy and executive and social-cognition deficits with posterior sparing.
Urination in inappropriate places is unconcerned and deliberate, not urge incontinence; ventricles are proportionate to atrophy.

key_clinical_evidence: Wife's history over 2 years: disinhibition (sexual remarks, urinating in the garden and the house, $22,000 withdrawn), apathy and loss of warmth, stereotyped television watching and a fixed food routine.
Prominent bilateral grasp and snout reflexes.
Severe executive and social-cognition deficits with mildly reduced memory and relatively preserved visuospatial function.
MRI: moderate frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with relative posterior sparing; Fazekas 2 small-vessel disease is a comorbidity, not the explanation of the syndrome.
Twelve years of sobriety, normal MCV and normal mammillary bodies and thalami argue against alcohol-related brain damage.
The frontal and anterior temporal pattern with relative posterior sparing makes Alzheimer disease less likely; an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.

Behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. Psychiatric disorders are the main mimics and are excluded on course and examination rather than on a single test. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured informant assessment, neuropsychological battery, reversible-cause blood tests and brain MRI. Optional: FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT, literature search.
metadata.notes: Probable bvFTD in a 61-year-old man with moderate small-vessel disease (Fazekas 2) and a remote alcohol use disorder in 12-year remission. Key teaching: the lobar frontal and anterior temporal pattern, normal mammillary bodies and thalami and the long sobriety separate bvFTD from vascular and alcohol-related mimics; vascular risk factors are treated as contributors.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change, disinhibition, and inappropriate behavior — 2 years

family_history: No family history of ALS or FTD

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T is a 61-year-old retired police sergeant with a history of remote alcohol use disorder (12 years sober, active AA member), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and treated obstructive sleep apnea who is brought to the neurology clinic by his wife. His wife has been his primary historian, as he minimizes all reported behavioral changes and insists he is 'fine.' She describes a 2-year history of progressive personality and behavioral transformation that she initially attributed to retirement stress. Approximately 2 years ago, Mr. T began to spend increasingly long periods watching the same sports content on television — up to 18 hours per day — and became enraged when interrupted. He has lost interest in grandchildren and friends, with whom he formerly had warm relationships. He has made several sexually inappropriate comments to his wife's sister and a female neighbor, which is completely out of character for a man his wife describes as having had 'strict moral values' throughout their 34-year marriage. He made two unauthorized withdrawals totaling $22,000 from their joint retirement account, the purpose of which he cannot or will not explain. He has urinated in the backyard on multiple occasions and twice inside the house in non-bathroom locations, each time appearing unconcerned about the behavior. He has developed a fixed eating routine, consuming chips and dip at the same time every day, becoming agitated when this is unavailable. His language has become more concrete — he gives one-word answers where he formerly was verbose. He has been sober for 12 years and still attends AA; his wife confirms he does not drink. He is adherent with CPAP and his wife confirms improved sleep quality.

neurological_exam.additional: Wife is clearly frustrated and distressed. She states her husband has been 'a completely different person' for the past 2 years. He watches football for 18 hours a day, eating chips and ignoring family. He made two large unauthorized withdrawals from their retirement savings for undisclosed purchases. He has urinated in the backyard and twice in inappropriate household locations. He has propositioned his wife's sister. The grasp reflex is prominent bilaterally. His prior alcohol use disorder is in long-term remission (12 years sober) and he is adherent with CPAP for his obstructive sleep apnea.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, mildly wide-based (possible cerebellar effect of remote alcohol use). No shuffling.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor. No rigidity. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric. No Babinski. Bilateral grasp and snout reflexes present; the grasp reflex is prominent.
